claim: Vibrotactile stimuli evoke two qualitatively distinctive cutaneous sensations: flutter (frequencies < 60 Hz) and vibratory hum (frequencies > 60 Hz).
source: The established view is that vibrotactile stimuli evoke two qualitatively distinctive cutaneous sensations, flutter (frequencies < 60 Hz) and vibratory hum (frequencies > 60 Hz), subserved by two distinct receptor types (Meissner's and Pacinian corpuscle, respectively), which may engage different neural processing pathways or channels and fulfil quite different biological roles.
evidence: This claim is presented as established knowledge in the field and is supported by citations in the broader context of the manuscript.

claim: Flutter and vibratory hum sensations are subserved by two distinct receptor types: Meissner's corpuscles and Pacinian corpuscles, respectively.
source: The established view is that vibrotactile stimuli evoke two qualitatively distinctive cutaneous sensations, flutter (frequencies < 60 Hz) and vibratory hum (frequencies > 60 Hz), subserved by two distinct receptor types (Meissner's and Pacinian corpuscle, respectively), which may engage different neural processing pathways or channels and fulfil quite different biological roles.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The two vibrotactile systems have been labelled as Pacinian and non-Pacinian channels in psychological and physiological literature.
source: In psychological and physiological literature, those two systems have been labelled as Pacinian and non-Pacinian channels.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the literature and terminology used in the field.

claim: Low-frequency spike trains in Pacinian afferents can induce a vibratory percept with the same low frequency attributes as sinusoidal stimuli of the same frequency.
source: However, we present evidence that low-frequency spike trains in Pacinian afferents can readily induce a vibratory percept with the same low frequency attributes as sinusoidal stimuli of the same frequency, thus demonstrating a universal frequency decoding system.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the Results section.

claim: Brief low-amplitude pulsatile mechanical stimuli can selectively activate Pacinian afferents.
source: We achieved this using brief low-amplitude pulsatile mechanical stimuli to selectively activate Pacinian afferents.
evidence: This is a methodological claim supported by experimental data showing threshold differences between afferent types.

claim: Spiking pattern, regardless of receptor type, determines vibrotactile frequency perception.
source: This indicates that spiking pattern, regardless of receptor type, determines vibrotactile frequency perception.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings showing similar frequency perception across different afferent types.

claim: This mechanism may underlie the constancy of vibrotactile frequency perception across different skin regions innervated by distinct afferent types.
source: This mechanism may underlie the constancy of vibrotactile frequency perception across different skin regions innervated by distinct afferent types.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: The sense of touch comprises a range of different perceptual qualities subserved by several distinct mechanoreceptor types and associated afferent nerve fibres in the skin.
source: The sense of touch comprises a range of different perceptual qualities subserved by several distinct mechanoreceptor types and associated afferent nerve fibres in the skin (Johnson, 2001; Vallbo and Johansson, 1984).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Different receptor types are tuned to different stimulus features and have distinct response profiles.
source: Observations that different receptor types are tuned to different stimulus features and have distinct response profiles have led researchers to conclude that different receptor types are the inputs to separate neural 'channels' dedicated to processing of those features (Bolanowski et al., 1994; Gescheider, 1976; Gescheider et al., 2004; Hyvarinen et al., 1968; Sretavan and Dykes, 1983).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: FAI (or RA) afferents innervating Meissner's corpuscles are preferentially activated at frequencies up to 60 Hz.
source: In the glabrous skin, there are two types of fast adapting (FA) afferents which at the threshold level display characteristic U-shaped tuning curves to sinusoidal vibrotactile stimuli: FAI (or RA) afferents innervating Meissner's corpuscles are preferentially activated at frequencies up to 60 Hz, while FAII (or Pacinian - PC) afferents innervating Pacinian corpuscles have much lower response thresholds, and are most sensitive to higher frequencies (>100 Hz) (Talbot et al., 1968).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: FAII (or Pacinian - PC) afferents innervating Pacinian corpuscles have much lower response thresholds and are most sensitive to higher frequencies (>100 Hz).
source: In the glabrous skin, there are two types of fast adapting (FA) afferents which at the threshold level display characteristic U-shaped tuning curves to sinusoidal vibrotactile stimuli: FAI (or RA) afferents innervating Meissner's corpuscles are preferentially activated at frequencies up to 60 Hz, while FAII (or Pacinian - PC) afferents innervating Pacinian corpuscles have much lower response thresholds, and are most sensitive to higher frequencies (>100 Hz) (Talbot et al., 1968).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: At about 60 Hz, there is a qualitative change in sensation from flutter to vibratory hum.
source: At the border between those two frequency domains, at about 60 Hz, there is a qualitative change in sensation from flutter to vibratory hum (Gescheider, 1976; LaMotte and Mountcastle, 1975; Talbot et al., 1968), which is used as further justification for psychophysical segregation into Pacinian and non-Pacinian channels.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The Pacinian channel may not possess neural circuits for processing low-frequency spiking patterns characteristic of low-frequency sinusoidal stimuli.
source: This scheme has engendered speculation that the Pacinian channel may not possess neural circuits for processing low-frequency spiking patterns characteristic of low-frequency sinusoidal stimuli, and therefore cannot produce a perceptual experience outside the high-frequency domain.
evidence: This is presented as speculation in the literature that the study aims to address.

claim: Sinusoidal stimuli inherently do not allow activation of FAII afferents at low frequencies.
source: There is a big gap in our knowledge, as sinusoidal stimuli inherently do not allow activation of FAII afferents at low frequencies and thus functionally are not representative for a wide variety of natural stimuli involving discrete mechanical transients associated with motor control or surface structures with low spatial frequency.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of sinusoidal stimuli based on known properties of FAII afferents.

claim: Low-frequency discharge in FAII afferents (the Pacinian channel) can cause conscious perception of a tactile stimulus at frequencies as low as 6 Hz.
source: By setting the amplitude of the mechanical pulses below the FAI activation threshold, we first established that low-frequency discharge in FAII afferents (the Pacinian channel) can indeed cause conscious perception of a tactile stimulus at frequencies as low as 6 Hz.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Detection thresholds for pulsatile stimuli on the finger were 1.3 (± 0.6 mean ± SD; n = 6) μm at 6 Hz.
source: For pulsatile stimuli, the detection thresholds on the finger were low at all frequencies: 1.3 (± 0.6 mean ± SD; n = 6) μm at the lowest (6 Hz) frequency and 0.7 (± 0.2; n = 6) μm at the highest (200 Hz) (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study, also shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Detection thresholds for pulsatile stimuli on the finger were 0.7 (± 0.2; n = 6) μm at 200 Hz.
source: For pulsatile stimuli, the detection thresholds on the finger were low at all frequencies: 1.3 (± 0.6 mean ± SD; n = 6) μm at the lowest (6 Hz) frequency and 0.7 (± 0.2; n = 6) μm at the highest (200 Hz) (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study, also shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Perceptual thresholds for pulsatile stimuli were well below response threshold for FAI afferents, regardless of frequency.
source: Regardless of the frequency, the perceptual thresholds for pulsatile stimuli were well below response threshold for FAI afferents (Johansson et al., 1982; Saal et al., 2017; Talbot et al., 1968), and thus could only have been mediated by the FAII afferents through the Pacinian channel.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data and cited knowledge about FAI afferent thresholds.

claim: Detection thresholds for pulsatile stimuli could only have been mediated by FAII afferents through the Pacinian channel.
source: Regardless of the frequency, the perceptual thresholds for pulsatile stimuli were well below response threshold for FAI afferents (Johansson et al., 1982; Saal et al., 2017; Talbot et al., 1968), and thus could only have been mediated by the FAII afferents through the Pacinian channel.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data and cited knowledge about afferent thresholds.

claim: Detection thresholds for sinusoidal stimuli were 28 (± 6; n = 6) μm at 6 Hz.
source: The detection thresholds for sinusoidal stimuli (Figure 1b) were considerably higher within flutter range frequencies and, as expected, steeply decreased with increasing frequency from 28 (± 6; n = 6) μm at 6 Hz to 0.7 (± 0.2; n = 6) μm at 200 Hz (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study, also shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Detection thresholds for sinusoidal stimuli were 0.7 (± 0.2; n = 6) μm at 200 Hz.
source: The detection thresholds for sinusoidal stimuli (Figure 1b) were considerably higher within flutter range frequencies and, as expected, steeply decreased with increasing frequency from 28 (± 6; n = 6) μm at 6 Hz to 0.7 (± 0.2; n = 6) μm at 200 Hz (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study, also shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The decrease in detection thresholds for sinusoidal stimuli with increasing frequency reflects a shift from activation of FAI afferents to activation of FAII afferents.
source: This reflects a shift from activation of FAI afferents, which have thresholds around 10–15 μm even at their characteristic frequencies, to activation of the much more sensitive FAII afferents which have thresholds for sinusoidal stimulation below 1 μm at their characteristic frequencies (Johansson et al., 1982; Saal et al., 2017; Talbot et al., 1968).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on cited knowledge about afferent thresholds.

claim: FAI afferents have thresholds around 10–15 μm even at their characteristic frequencies.
source: This reflects a shift from activation of FAI afferents, which have thresholds around 10–15 μm even at their characteristic frequencies, to activation of the much more sensitive FAII afferents which have thresholds for sinusoidal stimulation below 1 μm at their characteristic frequencies (Johansson et al., 1982; Saal et al., 2017; Talbot et al., 1968).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about FAI afferent properties.

claim: FAII afferents have thresholds for sinusoidal stimulation below 1 μm at their characteristic frequencies.
source: This reflects a shift from activation of FAI afferents, which have thresholds around 10–15 μm even at their characteristic frequencies, to activation of the much more sensitive FAII afferents which have thresholds for sinusoidal stimulation below 1 μm at their characteristic frequencies (Johansson et al., 1982; Saal et al., 2017; Talbot et al., 1968).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about FAII afferent properties.

claim: The PSE for a 20 Hz pulsatile test stimulus compared with pulsatile comparison stimuli was 20.0 (19.5–20.5; 95% confidence interval) Hz.
source: The PSEs obtained from the psychometric curves were very close to the physical frequencies of the presented test stimuli: 20.0 (19.5–20.5; 95% confidence interval, CI) Hz for the 20 Hz test, and 40.8 (39.8–41.7) Hz for the 40 Hz test stimulus (Figure 2; n = 12).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study, also shown in Figure 2.

claim: The PSE for a 40 Hz pulsatile test stimulus compared with pulsatile comparison stimuli was 40.8 (39.8–41.7) Hz.
source: The PSEs obtained from the psychometric curves were very close to the physical frequencies of the presented test stimuli: 20.0 (19.5–20.5; 95% confidence interval, CI) Hz for the 20 Hz test, and 40.8 (39.8–41.7) Hz for the 40 Hz test stimulus (Figure 2; n = 12).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study, also shown in Figure 2.

claim: Pulsatile stimuli evoked perceptions with a well-defined frequency, as indicated by narrow confidence interval values.
source: The narrow CI values indicate that pulsatile stimuli evoked perceptions with a well-defined frequency.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical data (narrow confidence intervals).

claim: The PSE for a 20 Hz sinusoidal test stimulus compared with sinusoidal comparison stimuli was 19.5 (18.8–20.2) Hz.
source: The PSE values obtained with sinusoidal stimuli (SS condition) using six sinusoidal comparison frequencies were 19.5 (18.8–20.2) Hz for the 20 Hz test and 41.7 (39.8–43.7) Hz for the 40 Hz test stimulus (Figure 2; n = 12).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study, also shown in Figure 2.

claim: The PSE for a 40 Hz sinusoidal test stimulus compared with sinusoidal comparison stimuli was 41.7 (39.8–43.7) Hz.
source: The PSE values obtained with sinusoidal stimuli (SS condition) using six sinusoidal comparison frequencies were 19.5 (18.8–20.2) Hz for the 20 Hz test and 41.7 (39.8–43.7) Hz for the 40 Hz test stimulus (Figure 2; n = 12).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study, also shown in Figure 2.

claim: There was no difference between pulsatile and sinusoidal stimuli types in PSE values (F(1, 11)=0.131, p=0.72).
source: Repeated measures two-way ANOVA indicated no difference between types of stimuli (pulsatile or sinusoidal) used (F(1, 11)=0.131, p=0.72).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis result from the experimental data.

claim: The PSE for a 20 Hz pulsatile test stimulus compared with sinusoidal comparison stimuli was 22.0 (19.7–24.4; 95% CI) Hz.
source: The PSE for the 20 Hz pulsatile test stimulus was 22.0 (19.7–24.4; 95% CI) Hz when determined in comparison to six sinusoidal frequencies (PS condition), which was no different from the 20 Hz stimulus (p=0.09, n = 12; one sample two-tailed t-test).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: The PSE for a 20 Hz pulsatile test stimulus compared with sinusoidal comparison stimuli was not different from 20 Hz (p=0.09, n = 12).
source: The PSE for the 20 Hz pulsatile test stimulus was 22.0 (19.7–24.4; 95% CI) Hz when determined in comparison to six sinusoidal frequencies (PS condition), which was no different from the 20 Hz stimulus (p=0.09, n = 12; one sample two-tailed t-test).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis result from the experimental data.

claim: Both pulsatile and sinusoidal low-frequency stimuli generate a percept of identical frequency within the flutter frequency range.
source: This indicates that both pulsatile and sinusoidal low-frequency stimuli generate a percept of identical frequency within the flutter frequency range.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing no statistical difference in PSE values.

claim: The PSE for a 40 Hz pulsatile test stimulus compared with sinusoidal comparison stimuli was 43.6 (39.8–47.4; 95% CI) Hz.
source: For 40 Hz pulsatile test stimulus, the PSE assessed in comparison with sinusoidal stimuli was 43.6 (39.8–47.4; 95% CI) Hz; again, this was not different from 40 Hz (p=0.06, n = 12; one sample two-tailed t-test).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: The PSE for a 40 Hz pulsatile test stimulus compared with sinusoidal comparison stimuli was not different from 40 Hz (p=0.06, n = 12).
source: For 40 Hz pulsatile test stimulus, the PSE assessed in comparison with sinusoidal stimuli was 43.6 (39.8–47.4; 95% CI) Hz; again, this was not different from 40 Hz (p=0.06, n = 12; one sample two-tailed t-test).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis result from the experimental data.

claim: Weber fractions mediated exclusively by FAII afferents within the flutter frequency range were just as low as Weber fractions determined with sinusoidal stimuli mediated predominantly by FAI afferents.
source: Weber fractions that were mediated exclusively by FAII afferents within the flutter frequency range were just as low as the Weber fractions determined with sinusoidal stimuli mediated predominantly by FAI afferents (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: FAII afferents provided frequency discrimination in the flutter range that was no different from sinusoidal stimuli predominantly mediated by FAI afferents (F(1, 11)=0.004, p=0.949).
source: Two-way repeated measures ANOVA indicated that the FAII afferents provided frequency discrimination in the flutter range that was no different from sinusoidal stimuli predominantly mediated by FAI afferents (F(1, 11)=0.004, p=0.949).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis result from the experimental data.

claim: There was an effect of frequency on Weber fraction size (F(1, 11)=29.00, p=0.0002).
source: However, there was an effect of frequency (F(1, 11)=29.00, p=0.0002) indicating that the size of the Weber fraction is affected by frequency and not afferent type providing this input.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis result from the experimental data.

claim: Weber fractions were lower at 40 Hz than at 20 Hz for both pulsatile and sinusoidal stimuli (0.21 vs 0.14 and 0.19 vs 0.15, respectively; n = 12).
source: Weber fractions were lower at the higher frequency (40 Hz) than they were at 20 Hz for both pulsatile and sinusoidal stimuli (0.21 vs 0.14 and 0.19 vs 0.15, respectively; n = 12).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: Low-frequency discharge of FAII afferents providing input to the Pacinian channel can mediate a clear perception of vibration with easily identifiable and distinguishable frequency characteristics within the flutter range.
source: Our study provides strong evidence that low-frequency discharge of FAII afferents providing input to the Pacinian channel can mediate a clear perception of vibration with easily identifiable and distinguishable frequency characteristics within the flutter range.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Frequency perception signalled exclusively by the activity of FAII afferents is directly comparable with the perceptual features of flutter frequency sensation evoked by corresponding sinusoidal stimuli that naturally activate predominantly FAI afferents.
source: We also established that frequency perception signalled exclusively by the activity of FAII afferents is directly comparable with the perceptual features of flutter frequency sensation evoked by corresponding sinusoidal stimuli that naturally activate predominantly FAI afferents (non-Pacinian channel).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: FAII afferents have large receptive fields.
source: As the afferent type and thus spatial properties of the population activation evoking this sensation (FAII afferents with large receptive fields) are different from that evoking the same frequency sense with low-amplitude sinusoidal stimulation (FAI afferents with small localised receptive fields), there are likely to be some differences in the quality of sensation beyond the frequency quality.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about FAII afferent properties.

claim: FAI afferents have small localised receptive fields.
source: As the afferent type and thus spatial properties of the population activation evoking this sensation (FAII afferents with large receptive fields) are different from that evoking the same frequency sense with low-amplitude sinusoidal stimulation (FAI afferents with small localised receptive fields), there are likely to be some differences in the quality of sensation beyond the frequency quality.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about FAI afferent properties.

claim: There are likely to be some differences in the quality of sensation beyond the frequency quality between FAII and FAI mediated sensations.
source: As the afferent type and thus spatial properties of the population activation evoking this sensation (FAII afferents with large receptive fields) are different from that evoking the same frequency sense with low-amplitude sinusoidal stimulation (FAI afferents with small localised receptive fields), there are likely to be some differences in the quality of sensation beyond the frequency quality.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on known differences in afferent properties.

claim: Pulsatile stimuli induce higher synchrony of activation across afferent fibres than sinusoidal stimuli due to their tighter time-envelope.
source: Differences may also relate to the higher synchrony of activation across afferent fibres induced with pulsatile stimuli than with sinusoidal stimuli, due to their tighter time-envelope.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of the stimuli used.

claim: The Weber fraction is generally around 0.2 in the flutter range.
source: The Weber fraction is generally used to characterise the smallest frequency differences reliably detected by subjects as a fraction of the comparison frequency. The Weber fraction is around 0.2 in the flutter range and at high frequencies has been reported to have a slightly higher value of around 0.3; however there is significant variation depending on methodology used (Bensmaïa et al., 2005; Goble and Hollins, 1994).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: At high frequencies, the Weber fraction has been reported to have a slightly higher value of around 0.3.
source: The Weber fraction is generally used to characterise the smallest frequency differences reliably detected by subjects as a fraction of the comparison frequency. The Weber fraction is around 0.2 in the flutter range and at high frequencies has been reported to have a slightly higher value of around 0.3; however there is significant variation depending on methodology used (Bensmaïa et al., 2005; Goble and Hollins, 1994).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: The discriminative ability of the Pacinian channel was not previously reported at frequencies outside the high-frequency range.
source: The discriminative ability of the Pacinian channel was not previously reported at frequencies outside the high-frequency range with which it is normally associated in vibrotactile perception.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the findings relative to existing literature.

claim: Weber fractions determined for the perceived frequency of vibration driven via the FAII and the FAI channels were a close match at both 20 and 40 Hz.
source: The Weber fractions determined for the perceived frequency of vibration driven via the FAII and the FAI channels were a close match at both frequencies tested (20 and 40 Hz), and show a similar decrease from 20 to 40 Hz.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Weber fractions show a similar decrease from 20 to 40 Hz for both FAII and FAI channels.
source: The Weber fractions determined for the perceived frequency of vibration driven via the FAII and the FAI channels were a close match at both frequencies tested (20 and 40 Hz), and show a similar decrease from 20 to 40 Hz.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Common neural mechanisms of frequency discrimination might be exploited by both FAII and FAI channels.
source: This suggests that common neural mechanisms of frequency discrimination might be exploited by both channels, as the existence of independent mechanisms having such close agreement at frequencies outside the usual operating range of one of the channels seems less likely.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the similarity of Weber fractions across channels.

claim: There is interaction between FAI and FAII inputs, as demonstrated by the assimilation effect where a frequency in the range of one channel can influence perceived frequency on the other channel.
source: Recent psychophysical evidence demonstrated that there is interaction between the FAI and FAII inputs, by showing the assimilation effect, where a frequency in the range of one channel can influence perceived frequency on the other channel (Kuroki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited evidence from another study.

claim: About 70–80% of rapidly adapting neurons in somatosensory cortex S1 show convergent inputs deriving from both FAI and FAII afferent classes.
source: It is known that about 70–80% of rapidly adapting neurons in somatosensory cortex S1 show convergent inputs deriving from both afferent classes, and it may be that these neurons are responsible for this generalised frequency processing.
evidence: This is cited knowledge about cortical neuron properties.

claim: Convergent S1 neurons may be responsible for generalised frequency processing.
source: It is known that about 70–80% of rapidly adapting neurons in somatosensory cortex S1 show convergent inputs deriving from both afferent classes, and it may be that these neurons are responsible for this generalised frequency processing.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on known cortical properties.

claim: Input from FAI afferents determines the cortical neuron response rate due to its net excitatory drive.
source: Saal et al. (2015) made an interesting observation that input from FAI afferents determines the cortical neuron response rate due to its net excitatory drive, while the more temporally-precise PC-channel has a balanced excitatory-inhibitory drive that can control the precise spike timing, which is useful in various encoding schemes (Birznieks and Vickery, 2017; Andrew Hires et al., 2015; Johansson and Birznieks, 2004; Prsa and Huber, 2018; Saal et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from another study.

claim: The PC-channel has a balanced excitatory-inhibitory drive that can control the precise spike timing.
source: Saal et al. (2015) made an interesting observation that input from FAI afferents determines the cortical neuron response rate due to its net excitatory drive, while the more temporally-precise PC-channel has a balanced excitatory-inhibitory drive that can control the precise spike timing, which is useful in various encoding schemes (Birznieks and Vickery, 2017; Andrew Hires et al., 2015; Johansson and Birznieks, 2004; Prsa and Huber, 2018; Saal et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from another study.

claim: The difference in excitatory-inhibitory drive between FAI and FAII inputs did not affect frequency perception in the current study.
source: This difference did not appear to affect frequency perception in the current study, as Weber fractions were found to be similar regardless of whether we used pulsatile stimuli exclusively activating FAII afferents in a time-controlled manner or used sinusoidal stimuli predominantly activating FAI afferents, presumably with less temporal precision due to the slow rising phase of the sinusoid.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Generalised neural processing for frequency, regardless of the source of afferent input, would support constancy of vibrotactile frequency perception across different skin regions innervated by different afferent types.
source: A consequence of generalised neural processing for frequency, regardless of the source of afferent input, is that it would support constancy of vibrotactile frequency perception across different skin regions innervated by different afferent types.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: Frequency perception on the hairy skin of the arm is not noticeably different from that of the glabrous skin.
source: For example, the frequency perception on the hairy skin of the arm is not noticeably different from that of the glabrous skin (Mahns et al., 2006; McIntyre et al., 2016), despite it having neither Meissner (FAI) nor Pacinian (FAII) receptors; instead vibrotactile stimuli are signalled by field units and hair follicle units (Vallbo et al., 1995).
evidence: This is cited evidence from other studies.

claim: Hairy skin of the arm has neither Meissner (FAI) nor Pacinian (FAII) receptors.
source: For example, the frequency perception on the hairy skin of the arm is not noticeably different from that of the glabrous skin (Mahns et al., 2006; McIntyre et al., 2016), despite it having neither Meissner (FAI) nor Pacinian (FAII) receptors; instead vibrotactile stimuli are signalled by field units and hair follicle units (Vallbo et al., 1995).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about skin receptor types.

claim: Vibrotactile stimuli on hairy skin are signalled by field units and hair follicle units.
source: For example, the frequency perception on the hairy skin of the arm is not noticeably different from that of the glabrous skin (Mahns et al., 2006; McIntyre et al., 2016), despite it having neither Meissner (FAI) nor Pacinian (FAII) receptors; instead vibrotactile stimuli are signalled by field units and hair follicle units (Vallbo et al., 1995).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about hairy skin receptor types.

claim: Natural stimulation is often of sufficiently high amplitude to activate multiple types of tactile afferents.
source: This also accords with natural stimulation, which is often of a sufficiently high amplitude to activate multiple types of tactile afferents (Johansson et al., 1982), and activate receptors across different skin types.
evidence: This is cited knowledge about natural tactile stimulation.

claim: FAII afferents and the Pacinian channel are well suited for detecting fast discrete mechanical transients with low repetition rate as might arise during object manipulation or exploration of surfaces with sparsely distributed sharp asperities or ridges.
source: Functionally, it means that FAII afferents and the Pacinian channel are well suited for detecting fast discrete mechanical transients with low repetition rate as might arise during object manipulation or exploration of surfaces with sparsely distributed sharp asperities or ridges.
evidence: This is a functional inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Low-frequency signals arising from FAII afferents are consciously perceived and easily discriminated.
source: The evidence that low-frequency signals arising from FAII afferents are consciously perceived and easily discriminated strongly suggests that they are biologically important and are likely to be utilised by neural circuits dedicated to motor control of the hand.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Low-frequency signals from FAII afferents are likely to be utilised by neural circuits dedicated to motor control of the hand.
source: The evidence that low-frequency signals arising from FAII afferents are consciously perceived and easily discriminated strongly suggests that they are biologically important and are likely to be utilised by neural circuits dedicated to motor control of the hand.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: The exquisite sensitivity of FAII afferents combined with their role in tactile perception and motor control makes them a useful target when designing haptic and teleoperated devices.
source: In regard to new technology development, the exquisite sensitivity of FAII afferents combined with their role in tactile perception and motor control makes them a useful target when designing haptic and teleoperated devices.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about technological applications based on the findings.

claim: Perception of vibrotactile frequency depends on the discharge pattern of the active afferents, rather than the afferent type that is active.
source: It has become evident that perception of vibrotactile frequency depends on the discharge pattern of the active afferents, rather than the afferent type that is active.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Much of the observed functional dichotomy between Pacinian and non-Pacinian channels may relate to behavioural interpretations of the stimulus rather than to the type of receptor that the signal originates from.
source: These new findings raise questions about whether much of the observed functional dichotomy between Pacinian and non-Pacinian channels relates to behavioural interpretations of the stimulus rather than to the type of receptor that the signal originates from.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the findings.

claim: A universal frequency decoding system would help explain the perceptual constancy of vibrotactile frequency perception across distinct human skin regions and types.
source: In addition, our proposed universal frequency decoding system would help explain the perceptual constancy of vibrotactile frequency perception which is a prominent problem in tactile system where distinct human skin regions and types (e.g. glabrous and hairy) functionally encode the same physical features of stimuli using remarkably different receptor types tuned for different stimulus features.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: These findings are consistent with the growing evidence of extensive convergence of inputs from different afferent types onto neurons in the primary somatosensory cortex.
source: These findings are consistent with the growing evidence of extensive convergence of inputs from different afferent types onto neurons in the primary somatosensory cortex.
evidence: This is a statement connecting the findings to existing literature.

claim: These findings indicate the need to review the functional and neurophysiological basis on which processing of vibrotactile stimuli is attributed to Pacinian and non-Pacinian channels.
source: Finally, these findings indicate the need to review the functional and neurophysiological basis on which processing of vibrotactile stimuli is attributed to Pacinian and non-Pacinian channels.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the implications of the findings for the field.

source: Research participants were healthy volunteers aged 20 to 26 years without any known history of neurological disorders which would affect the somatosensory system.
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

source: There were six participants (four female) in the detection threshold experiments and 12 (6 female) in the frequency perception experiments.

claim: There were 12 participants (6 female) in the frequency perception experiments.
source: There were six participants (four female) in the detection threshold experiments and 12 (6 female) in the frequency perception experiments.

source: Five participants were in both experiments.

claim: A stereotyped brief pulsatile mechanical stimulus with a protraction time of only 2 ms was used to control the spiking pattern in recruited afferents.
source: A stereotyped brief pulsatile mechanical stimulus with a protraction time of only 2 ms was used to control the spiking pattern in recruited afferents (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

claim: Each mechanical pulse generated only a single time-controlled spike in responding afferents because the duration of the mechanical stimulus was comparable to the refractory period of the action potential.
source: As the duration of the mechanical stimulus was comparable to the refractory period of the action potential, each mechanical stimulation event generated only a single time-controlled spike in responding afferents (Birznieks and Vickery, 2017).
evidence: This is a methodological claim supported by citation and physiological knowledge.

claim: Each mechanical pulse is a reproducible and uniform event which ensures that the same population of afferents will be excited regardless of the rate at which these pulses are repeated.
source: Each mechanical pulse is a reproducible and uniform event which ensures that the same population of afferents will be excited regardless of the rate at which these pulses are repeated.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the properties of the stimulus.

claim: Detection thresholds were measured for pulsatile and sinusoidal stimuli at four frequencies: 6, 24, 100 and 200 Hz.
source: Detection thresholds were measured for pulsatile and sinusoidal stimuli at four frequencies: 6, 24, 100 and 200 Hz.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The threshold was defined as the intensity at which the stimulus could be correctly identified for 82% of trials.
source: We defined the threshold as the intensity at which the stimulus could be correctly identified for 82% of trials, and was given by the mean of the posterior distribution function.
evidence: This is a methodological definition used in the study.

claim: For each threshold estimate, 41 trials were conducted.
source: For each threshold estimate, 41 trials were conducted.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: The amplitude of all pulsatile stimuli was 3 µm which was approximately three times the sensory threshold.
source: The amplitude of all pulsatile stimuli was 3 µm which was approximately three times the sensory threshold found in our detection threshold experiment.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental stimulus parameters.

claim: At 3 µm amplitude, only Pacinian (FAII) afferents are expected to respond.
source: At this amplitude, we expect only Pacinian (FAII) afferents to respond, as threshold for recruitment of FAI afferents, even at their preferred frequency within the flutter range, is no lower than 10 µm.
evidence: This is an inference based on known afferent thresholds and experimental data.

claim: The threshold for recruitment of FAI afferents, even at their preferred frequency within the flutter range, is no lower than 10 µm.
source: At this amplitude, we expect only Pacinian (FAII) afferents to respond, as threshold for recruitment of FAI afferents, even at their preferred frequency within the flutter range, is no lower than 10 µm.
evidence: This is cited knowledge about FAI afferent thresholds.

claim: The shape (acceleration profile) of the pulsatile stimulus used in this study corresponds to a waveform of sinusoidal stimulus > 250 Hz.
source: The shape (acceleration profile) of the pulsatile stimulus used in this study corresponds to a waveform of sinusoidal stimulus > 250 Hz.
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus properties.

claim: For stimuli at > 250 Hz frequency, FAI afferents typically respond at amplitudes about 10 fold higher than the 3 µm stimuli used for selective FAII afferent activation in this study.
source: For stimuli at this frequency, FAI afferents typically respond at amplitudes about 10 fold higher than the 3 µm stimuli used for selective FAII afferent activation in this study (Freeman and Johnson, 1982; Johansson et al., 1982; Saal et al., 2017; Talbot et al., 1968).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about FAI afferent response properties.

claim: An FAII afferent responded to 3 μm pulsatile stimuli at 20 imp/s, as shown in Figure 5a.
source: The response of one FAII afferent recorded by microneurography in a human subject, evoked by 3 μm pulsatile stimuli at 20 imp/s, is shown in Figure 5a.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: An FAI afferent responded to 20 Hz sinusoidal stimuli at 20 imp/s, as shown in Figure 5b.
source: For comparison, the response of one FAI afferent to 20 Hz sinusoidal stimuli also responding at 20 imp/s is shown in Figure 5b.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The FAI afferent started responding sporadically at 30 μm pulsatile stimulus amplitude.
source: The FAI afferent starts responding sporadically at 30 μm and becomes entrained 1:1 with a stimulus amplitude of 35 μm.
evidence: This is experimental data from microneurography recordings.

claim: The FAI afferent became entrained 1:1 with a pulsatile stimulus amplitude of 35 μm.
source: The FAI afferent starts responding sporadically at 30 μm and becomes entrained 1:1 with a stimulus amplitude of 35 μm.
evidence: This is experimental data from microneurography recordings.

claim: Firing pattern is identical regardless of stimulus or afferent type, as shown in Figure 5 panels A, B and E.
source: Note that firing pattern in A, B and E is identical regardless of stimulus or afferent type.
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Amplitude of sinusoidal or pulsatile stimuli had no effect on PSE or Weber's fractions, indicating that subjects can readily judge frequency while ignoring any intensity cues.
source: The data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 show that amplitude of the sinusoidal or pulsatile stimuli had no effect on PSE or Weber's fractions indicating that subjects can readily judge frequency while ignoring any intensity cues.
evidence: This is a conclusion from control experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.
